front_blocks.md: Define **lattice enthalpy**

back_blocks.md: **Lattice enthalpy** (Δ<sub>latt</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>) is the enthalpy change when **1 mole** of an ionic compound is formed from its **gaseous ions** under standard conditions.
It is always **exothermic** (negative) due to strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

cards.front_md: Define **lattice enthalpy**
cards.back_md:
**Lattice enthalpy** (Δ<sub>latt</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>) is the enthalpy change when **1 mole** of an ionic compound is formed from its **gaseous ions** under standard conditions.

It is always **exothermic** (negative) due to strong electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

front_blocks.md: Why is **lattice enthalpy** always exothermic?

back_blocks.md: Energy is **released** when gaseous ions combine to form an **ionic solid lattice**.
Strong **electrostatic forces of attraction** between oppositely charged ions stabilise the lattice, making it much more stable than the gaseous ions.

cards.front_md: Why is **lattice enthalpy** always exothermic?
cards.back_md:

Strong **electrostatic forces of attraction** between oppositely charged ions stabilise the lattice, making it much more stable than the gaseous ions.

front_blocks.md: Define **standard enthalpy change of atomisation**

back_blocks.md: **Standard enthalpy change of atomisation** (Δ<sub>at</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>) is the enthalpy change when **1 mole of gaseous atoms** is formed from its **element** in its standard state.
It is always **endothermic** (positive) as energy is required to break bonds.

front_blocks.md: Define: **first electron affinity**

back_blocks.md: **First electron affinity** (Δ<sub>ea</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>) is the enthalpy change when **1 mole of electrons** is added to **1 mole of gaseous atoms** to form **1 mole of gaseous ions** with a 1− charge.
The first electron affinity is always **exothermic**.

front_blocks.md: Why is the **second electron affinity** of oxygen **endothermic**?

back_blocks.md: Adding a second electron to an already **negatively charged ion** (O<sup>-</sup>) requires overcoming a large **electrostatic repulsion**.\nThis requires a large input of energy, making the process endothermic.

front_blocks.md: What is a **Born-Haber cycle**?

back_blocks.md: A **Born-Haber cycle** is a specific application of Hess's law for ionic compounds.
It allows lattice enthalpy to be calculated indirectly by linking the enthalpy of formation to all other measurable enthalpy changes.

front_blocks.md: List the **enthalpy changes** included in a Born-Haber cycle for NaCl, in the order they appear going from elements to gaseous ions.

back_blocks.md:
1. Enthalpy of atomisation of Na
2. Enthalpy of atomisation of Cl
3. First ionisation energy of Na
4. First electron affinity of Cl
The cycle is completed by the **enthalpy of formation** of NaCl and the **lattice enthalpy**.

front_blocks.md: In a Born-Haber cycle, energy **increases** going **..........**

front_blocks.md: Define **polarisation** (in the context of ionic compounds)

back_blocks.md: **Polarisation** occurs when a cation distorts the electron cloud of an anion, pulling electron density towards itself.
This introduces **covalent character** into what would otherwise be a purely ionic bond.

front_blocks.md: What causes a difference between **theoretical** and **experimental** lattice enthalpies?

back_blocks.md: The theoretical value assumes a **perfect ionic model** with 100% spherical ions and purely electrostatic attraction.
In reality, **polarisation** introduces covalent character, causing the experimental lattice enthalpy to be more exothermic than predicted.

front_blocks.md: What is **polarising power**?

back_blocks.md: **Polarising power** is the ability of a **cation** to distort the electron cloud of an anion.
It increases with smaller ionic radius and higher ionic charge, as these give a greater **charge density**.

front_blocks.md: Which cation has greater **polarising power**: Li<sup>+</sup> or K<sup>+</sup>? Explain.

back_blocks.md: **Li**<sup>**+**</sup> has greater polarising power.
Li<sup>+</sup> has a **smaller ionic radius** than K<sup>+</sup>, giving it a higher **charge density**. A higher charge density means a greater ability to distort the electron cloud of an anion.

front_blocks.md: What property of an **anion** determines how easily it is polarised?

back_blocks.md: The **ionic radius** of the anion determines its **polarisability**.
Larger anions are more easily polarised as their outer electrons are further from the nucleus and less strongly attracted, making the electron cloud more easily distorted.

front_blocks.md: Define **enthalpy of solution**

back_blocks.md: **Enthalpy of solution** (Δ<sub>sol</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>) is the enthalpy change when **1 mole** of an ionic substance **dissolves** in sufficient water to form an **infinitely dilute solution**.
It can be exothermic or endothermic.

front_blocks.md: Define **enthalpy of hydration**

back_blocks.md: **Enthalpy of hydration** (Δ<sub>hyd</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>) is the enthalpy change when **1 mole of a specified gaseous ion** dissolves in sufficient water to form an infinitely dilute solution.
Hydration enthalpies are always **exothermic**.

front_blocks.md: Why is the enthalpy of hydration always **exothermic**?

back_blocks.md: Energy is **released** when **ion-dipole attractions** form between the gaseous ions and polar water molecules.
The δ− oxygen of water attracts positive ions and the δ+ hydrogen atoms attract negative ions.

front_blocks.md: What are the **three factors** that determine whether an ionic solid is soluble?

2. The **enthalpy change of solution** (Δ<sub>sol</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>)
3. The **temperature** of the water (in K)
Solubility is thermodynamically spontaneous when ΔS<sub>total</sub> is positive.

cards.front_md: What are the **three factors** that determine whether an ionic solid is soluble?
cards.back_md:
1. The **entropy of the system** (ΔS<sub>system</sub>)
2. The **enthalpy change of solution** (Δ<sub>sol</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>)
3. The **temperature** of the water (in K)

Solubility is thermodynamically spontaneous when ΔS<sub>total</sub> is positive.

front_blocks.md: **True or False?**
Increasing pressure always shifts the equilibrium to the right.

back_blocks.md: **False.**

An endothermic Δ<sub>sol</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup> can still allow dissolution if the **entropy increase of the system** is large enough to make ΔS<sub>total</sub> positive, as seen with NH<sub>4</sub>NO<sub>3</sub> dissolving in water.

front_blocks.md: When MgCl<sub>2</sub> dissolves, why must the Cl<sup>-</sup> hydration enthalpy be **doubled** in the calculation?

back_blocks.md: MgCl<sub>2</sub> contains **two** Cl<sup>-</sup> ions per formula unit.
Therefore 2 moles of Cl<sup>-</sup> ions are hydrated per mole of MgCl<sub>2</sub>, so Δ<sub>hyd</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup>[Cl<sup>-</sup>] must be **multiplied by 2**.

front_blocks.md: What happens to the **entropy of water** when ions become hydrated?

back_blocks.md: The entropy of water **decreases**.
Water molecules become more **ordered** as they arrange themselves around the cations and anions to form ion-dipole bonds.

front_blocks.md: Complete the expression for total entropy change during dissolution:
ΔS<sub>total</sub> = ΔS<sub>system</sub> **..........**

back_blocks.md: ΔS<sub>total</sub> = ΔS<sub>system</sub> **− Δ**<sub>**sol**</sub>**H / T**
Where T is the temperature in kelvin. This shows that a positive ΔS<sub>system</sub> and/or a negative Δ<sub>sol</sub>H (exothermic) both favour dissolution.

front_blocks.md: How does **increasing ionic radius** affect **lattice enthalpy**?

back_blocks.md: Increasing ionic radius makes lattice enthalpy **less exothermic**
Larger ions have more **spread out charge** and are **further apart**, weakening the electrostatic forces of attraction between oppositely charged ions.

front_blocks.md: Why is the lattice enthalpy of **CaO** more exothermic than that of **KCl**?

back_blocks.md: Ca<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> have **greater ionic charges** than K<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>-</sup>.
The stronger electrostatic forces between the more highly charged ions release more energy when the lattice forms. Ca<sup>2+</sup> and O<sup>2-</sup> are also smaller ions, reinforcing the effect.

front_blocks.md: How does **ionic charge** affect the **enthalpy of hydration**?

back_blocks.md: A higher ionic charge gives a greater **charge density**, which attracts water molecules more strongly.
This results in a **more exothermic** enthalpy of hydration, e.g. Mg<sup>2+</sup> has a more negative Δ<sub>hyd</sub>H<sup>ꝋ</sup> than Ba<sup>2+</sup>.
